A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAIRL research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v3 Appendix F reports original Gridworld experiments comparing Uniform Sampling with behavior cloning under deterministic, stochastic, and obstacle conditions.

after.justification: v4 retains the Gridworld experiments in Appendix G.2 and adds numerical studies of equilibrium ambiguity and Nash versus QRE observations in Figures 2–3 and Appendix G.1.

M1.justification: The Uniform Sampling algorithm, empirical estimators, entropy-regularized reward construction, and Random Max Gap procedure are retained. The revised identifiability analysis establishes different theoretical conditions rather than a revised learning algorithm.

E1.justification: v4 adds an absorbing-state coordination Markov game evaluated using Nash and QRE expert observations. This is a limited extension of toy-game coverage; the original 3×3 Gridworld and its transition-change and obstacle scenarios remain.

E2.justification: Figure 3 introduces a direct empirical comparison between recovery from unregularized Nash observations and recovery from QRE observations. The original Uniform Sampling versus behavior cloning comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix G.1 adds a diagnostic protocol that computes initial-state experts, enumerates recovered equilibria, randomly selects an equilibrium for exploitability assessment, and measures equilibrium counts and Pearson/Spearman reward correlations. The retained Gridworld evaluation settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 2–3 add direct numerical analyses of two central questions: whether feasible rewards introduce exploitable equilibria, and whether QRE observations better preserve equilibrium structure and reward relationships. v3 supported these issues through analytical examples rather than these empirical diagnostics.

E5.justification: Appendix G.1 newly specifies 10,000 repetitions for the added diagnostics. Figure 2 includes error bars without defining their interpretation. There is no reported increase in repetitions for the retained Gridworld experiments.

E6.justification: v4 adds findings that Nash-based recovery can introduce new equilibria with positive exploitability, while QRE-based recovery produces no new pure equilibria in the tested example and higher Pearson/Spearman reward correlations. The original Gridworld curves and comparative findings are retained in Figure 4.

T1.justification: v4 adds a discounted-Nash-gap hardness construction, strengthens the optimality definition with a supremum over recovered equilibria, and explicitly defines a regularized criterion. Section 4 and Appendix F replace v3's single-observation zero-sum identifiability argument with multiple-environment rank conditions, induced-transition sample bounds, and estimation-stability results.

C1.justification: v4 foregrounds reward identifiability as a core research question and adds a quantified worst-case Nash-gap claim. It replaces v3's claim that separable zero-sum structure supplies identification without another expert with conditional identification claims involving two environments and rank assumptions.

C2.justification: v4 explains QRE benefits through exploration and coverage, and revises the interpretation of identifiability around opponent-dependent average rewards and additional observations. Its conclusion also explicitly discusses restrictive generative-model access and the different coverage requirements of offline multi-agent learning.

D1.justification: Appendix G.1 adds descriptions of initial-state Nash solving, iterative QRE policy updates, and equilibrium selection for the new diagnostics. The existing Gridworld and Max Gap implementation descriptions remain. Specific solver choices and QRE regularization values for the new studies are not supplied.

R1.justification: The expanded Appendix B develops substantially fuller comparisons concerning identifiability, large-state IRL, and bounded rationality. It adds discussion of directly relevant concurrent work by Liao et al. (2025), alongside Kim et al. (2021), Lazzati et al. (2024a), and Wu et al. (2022), beyond relocating the earlier related-work section.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around two research questions. Main sections are consolidated, related work and pure-Nash analysis move into appendices, and an appendix contents page and comprehensive notation guide improve navigation.

P2.justification: v4 adds a feasible-set illustration and two multipart diagnostic figures, replaces the short notation table with a full-page glossary, and adopts a different conference layout and typography. The original Gridworld plots and environment diagrams are retained as Figures 4–5.

improvement.justification: v4 adds relevant numerical support and clearer organization, but its revised central theory contains material inconsistencies. Proposition 4.3 requires rank 2|S|(|B|+1)-1, whereas Proposition F.5 requires |S|(|B|+1)-1; Theorems 4.2 and F.2 also disagree on linear versus quadratic state dependence. These conflicts limit confidence in the replacement identifiability analysis, leaving the net quality change uncertain.
